text: My biggest issue with CS-7641 was honestly how unclear the target was on the written work. The course is very report-heavy, and in a summer term that gets old fast. I took it because it’s required for the degree, and trying to fit the class around short evening study sessions was rough when every assignment seemed to turn into “one more writeup section” with a rubric that still felt vague. I never felt like I fully knew what counted as enough analysis versus overexplaining obvious ML results, and the feedback from Dr. Park’s course was so sparse that by the time you got a real sense of what they wanted, you were already deep into the next submission. The week I remember most was the assignment/exam stretch where I was revising a long report late at night and still wasn’t sure whether I was being graded more on model performance or on how I framed the discussion of errors and tuning choices. That kind of thing was tiring in a compressed term. It’s mostly individual work too, which I usually like, but here it meant you just kind of sat with your confusion and kept typing. That said, the actual content in Machine Learning was worth learning, and it did feel relevant to what I expected a core ML class should cover. Even when I was annoyed, I could see why the topics mattered and why the course is in the program. My expectations were basically “this will be demanding but structured,” and it was definitely the first part more than the second. I got through it, learned useful material, and was more exhausted than impressed by the course design.
note: The review strongly criticizes vague rubrics, unclear grading targets, and sparse feedback around written assignments, indicating negative (not neutral) sentiment about assessment design.

text: CS-6400 / Database Systems Concepts and Design was useful in the sense that it covered material I actually needed for my specialization, but I honestly wouldn’t recommend it unless you really have to take it. I took it while working full time, and that probably shaped a lot of my experience. It starts off like a pretty accessible intro service course, so at first I thought, okay, this is manageable. Then the workload jumped hard once the database-design assignments and reports started piling up. The part I still remember is one week when a project report and an exam landed basically on top of each other, and I was up late trying to clean up schema diagrams while also second-guessing what level of explanation the report wanted. That was kind of the recurring problem for me: the instructions often left too much room for interpretation, and I never felt fully sure whether I was giving what they wanted or just what seemed reasonable to me. The LMS itself was actually fine. Submitting things was smooth and I never had technical issues, which mattered because I was usually turning stuff in after work and didn’t have time for platform drama. Grade-wise I ended up in the C range, and I’m still not totally convinced that reflected what I understood by the end. Some of that is on me because the deadlines stacked up worse than I expected, but some of it was how report-heavy the course was. I learned from it, especially around thinking through schema choices, but it was a frustrating class to get through.

text: I took CS-7641 Machine Learning with Dr. Chen in the middle of a pretty brutal semester while working full time, and honestly the fit was bad for me. I code a lot for work, so implementing experiments and writing the reports was manageable, but the class assumes more theory intuition than I had. Dr. Chen is actually very good at explaining the big concepts, but when I got stuck trying to connect that to model-tuning choices in the assignments, the examples felt too thin to bail me out. The tooling/setup was also way more effort than it was worth. I spent an annoying amount of time getting everything to run cleanly just to do fairly standard experiment work, which was kind of a pain. Feedback was uneven too: one report got thoughtful comments I could use, another felt like it was graded by a completely different standard. Group work helped when the team clicked, and mine mostly did, so I’ll give it that. I learned a lot, no question, but I really didn’t enjoy taking this course and I can’t recommend it unless your theory background is already stronger than mine.

text: CS-6250, Computer Networks with Dr. Chen, was one of those classes where I was usually watching the recordings late at night instead of showing up live, because I work full time and didn’t have a lot of study hours in a normal week. The lectures themselves were actually pretty clear. When Dr. Chen walked through a topic step by step, I usually understood what he was saying in the moment. What threw me off was that the course seemed to expect more background than the description suggested. I remember getting confused really early on during the first stretch of material, because I had come in thinking it would build a bit more gradually from the easier prereq, and instead I felt like everyone else already knew the logic behind half the discussion. That early confusion kind of set the tone for me for most of the term. The work was also heavier than I expected, especially the reports. Not impossible, just very time-consuming in a way that is rough if you’re fitting the class around a job. I barely passed, and that sounds right for how the semester felt. A lot of my exam prep was basically trying to turn scattered notes, recordings, and forum clarifications into something coherent. One thing that saved the course for me was office hours. I don’t say that casually. I relied on them a lot once I realized I was not going to fix my understanding by rewatching lectures alone. The forum was useful for small clarifications too, but office hours were where things finally clicked. I also had more stress than necessary from the platform/tool side of the class. Nothing dramatic, just enough quirks and little issues that it kept eating time I didn’t really have. So my experience was mixed in a pretty straightforward way: Dr. Chen explained things clearly, but the class was harder and more assumption-heavy than advertised, and if I hadn’t used office hours, I probably would not have made it through.

text: CS-6250 Computer Networks was weirder for me than I expected. I’m usually fine in theory-heavy classes, proofs, that kind of thing, and I went in thinking this would be basically an easier follow-on from the prereq. It wasn’t harder exactly, just different. More systems-y in a way I never fully got comfortable with. Still, it actually filled in some missing basics for me better than I thought it would, especially around how the protocols fit together instead of just seeing them as vocab words. I started the semester pretty locked in and went to lecture consistently. Then somewhere around the late-semester routing/unit stretch, when we were looking at packet traces and I realized I could mechanically identify what was happening without really knowing why one approach was chosen over another, my attendance kind of dropped off. I had enough time for the class overall. Motivation was the less consistent part. The main thing I remember is that help felt thin. Not hostile, just thin. Questions about assignments or what counted as “enough” collaboration never felt answered in a way that made me confident I was doing the right thing. That part was honestly kind of a mess. I never knew if discussing debugging at a high level was normal or if that was already too much. Because of that I mostly worked alone, which probably made the networking assignments feel more annoying than they needed to. Grading itself was actually clearer than I expected. Scores came back fast, which I appreciated, and the rubric categories were usually straightforward enough to tell where I lost points. But the comments were often so brief that they didn’t help much for the next assignment. So I’d know I missed something in a protocol handling case, but not really get the why beyond a line or two. Also the assessments and lectures didn’t always feel lined up. Lecture could stay fairly conceptual, then homework/project stuff would suddenly expect a much more practical comfort level. Coming from the easier prereq, that gap stood out. Not impossible, just kind of jarring. I learned a decent amount, yeah, but I spent a lot of the semester feeling like I was supposed to infer the workflow on my own.
note: The reviewer says help felt "thin," questions weren’t answered clearly, and collaboration guidance was a mess, indicating negative support.
overall_note: Both aspects are clearly discussed and the declared sentiments align with the review.

text: CS-7641 Machine Learning was useful, but honestly I didn’t enjoy it much, and I’d only tell someone to take it if they go in already prepared and ready to teach themselves parts of it. Dr. Miller’s lectures were actually not the problem for me. He speaks clearly, the pacing is decent, and when I was sitting there taking notes it all felt understandable enough. That’s what made the class so frustrating. In lecture, things sound manageable. Then the assignments or project work hit and suddenly the expectations feel way less clear than the presentation did. It was one of those classes where I kept thinking “wait, what exactly are we being graded on here?” even though I had pages of notes. That disconnect was the main thing I remember. Also, there are only a few assessments, which sounds nice until you realize every single one carries a ton of weight, so if one goes badly you just feel cooked for a while. I ended with a solid B and that felt about right for the amount of effort I put in, but it definitely wasn’t a relaxed B. More like a “spent too many evenings tweaking things and still not fully sure what they wanted” B. The worst part was the feedback timing. By the time anything useful came back, we were already deep into the next thing, so it didn’t really help me adjust. That drove me crazy more than I expected. I remember waiting for comments on one assignment while trying to make decisions for the next part of the course, and it just felt like guessing with higher stakes than it needed to be. Most of the actual help came from other students comparing notes, not from staff. If you weren’t in some kind of group chat or talking to classmates, I think this class would feel way harder. I took it because it’s required for the degree, and I do think the material matters. I’m not saying it’s a bad course in the sense of being pointless. It’s definitely relevant, and I can see why it’s a mid-program core course. I just think the experience of taking it was more aggravating than it needed to be, mostly because the course felt clearer on the surface than it was when you actually had to perform under pressure. That part really got under my skin.
note: The reviewer repeatedly says expectations and grading criteria felt unclear, with a disconnect between understandable lectures and confusing assignments/projects.
overall_note: The review clearly expresses negative clarity due to unclear expectations, grading, and delayed feedback.

text: I took CS-6250 Computer Networks with Prof. Haddad while working full time, which probably made some parts hit harder than they would have otherwise. I was also pretty new to the discipline, basically still learning the basics, and the class definitely felt like it expected more background than the description let on. Not impossible, just one of those courses where everyone else seems to already know why a protocol behaves a certain way and you’re still trying to keep the layers straight. I did learn a lot, weirdly enough. By the end I could read traces without feeling totally lost, and I understood networking in a much less hand-wavy way than before. But I honestly didn’t enjoy most of the experience. There were only a few assessments, and that made every single one feel high stakes. If one went sideways, it really mattered. The most frustrating part for me was the grading. I ended up with a C, and I’m still not really sure that matched what I actually understood. The feedback quality bounced around a lot depending on the assignment—sometimes decent, sometimes so thin that it didn’t help me figure out what I’d done wrong. On one networking assignment I lost points after getting the expected behavior in my output, and the comment was basically just that my approach wasn’t what they wanted. I’m still not clear on what the rubric was there, which was rough when there weren’t many chances to recover. Also, minor but not minor when you’re tired after work: the tooling/setup side was a pain. I spent too much time wondering whether I was debugging my own mistake or just fighting the environment. That kind of thing really drains you in a class like this. Honestly this course works better if you have a study group. I mostly kept up by comparing notes with other people and sanity-checking what the assignments were even asking for. I’d recommend it if you prepare ahead and maybe brush up before the semester starts, but I wouldn’t call it beginner-friendly just because the catalog sort of implies that.
note: They describe unclear rubrics, losing points despite expected output, and inconsistent/thin feedback, indicating poor transparency.

text: I took CS-6200 / Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems in the middle of a pretty brutal semester, and I’m still a little unsure how I feel about it. text: CS-6200 / Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems was a required course for my track, and I took it while juggling full-time work plus a couple of other pretty demanding classes. So honestly I remember the pacing more than anything. It was a lot, but in a good way most weeks. Dr. Park’s lectures were actually easier to stick with than another course I had the same term, mostly because even when the material got dense, it felt organized enough that I could recover after a long workday. The biggest frustration for me was the grading rubric. I never totally knew what counted as “enough” on some parts of the projects, and the collaboration expectations were fuzzier than I wanted. Not a disaster, just the kind of thing that makes you second guess whether you’re doing operating systems work wrong or just reading the spec differently. I ended up with a solid B, which felt fair for the amount of effort I could realistically put in. One thing I do remember clearly: I went to office hours once after getting stuck reading through a project spec, and Dr. Park took a few minutes to sketch out what the scheduler section was really asking for. That helped a lot. The support side was good in that sense. Detailed comments too, when grades finally came back. Just… not fast. Email was especially rough near deadlines, and by the time I got a reply once, I had already submitted. Still, I was genuinely glad I took it. Hard course, definitely not light, but more accessible than I expected for a systems class.

text: I’d still recommend CS-6400 with Dr. Singh, especially as a last-semester advanced elective, but I was more annoyed by the way it ran than I expected. What I remember most is that the course never quite felt settled week to week. Not chaotic exactly, just a little hard to track, and that got old fast. I kept double-checking what was due and what counted for what, which is not how I wanted to spend the semester. The slides were fine in the sense that they covered the material, but they didn’t really stick with me, so I ended up relying more on the project docs and my own notes than on lecture itself. That said, feedback came back quickly enough that if you messed something up early, you could actually fix it on the next checkpoint instead of finding out at the end, which I appreciated. I went in a little worried because I’m much more comfortable with proofs than systems work, and honestly it filled in some gaps better than I thought it would. I’m not saying it suddenly made me a systems person, but it didn’t feel like I was drowning either. The grading rubrics for the design writeups helped more than the lectures did, weirdly. The class is definitely project-heavy, but then the exams still carry a lot of weight, so I never totally relaxed. Time pressure was manageable most weeks, though. Most weeks. I guess that’s why I’m mixed on it, because I did learn a lot more practical database thinking than I expected, and I’d still tell people to take it, but I was also frustrated pretty often by the organization, and that part never really stopped bothering me.

text: CS-6200 with Dr. Singh was harder than I expected for a mid-program core course, and not really in a way that felt well-shaped. I took it in my first semester, and I had enough time to keep up on paper, but my motivation was all over the place because the class itself felt uneven week to week. Some lectures clicked, then the next week I’d be staring at project requirements wondering how we got from the slides to that. The worst stretch for me was the assignment week around kernel implementation stuff where the forums were full of people asking basic setup questions and the TAs were basically doing damage control. I lost an embarrassing amount of time just getting the tooling to behave on my machine, which made me way more irritated than the actual OS concepts did. Office hours helped sometimes, but it also felt like you had to reverse-engineer expectations from scattered answers. What bothered me most was that the assessments didn’t really line up with how the material was delivered. The course wanted a certain kind of confidence in implementation-heavy work that I don’t think the lectures consistently built. And since most of it was individual, there wasn’t much of that “figure it out together” energy that usually saves a rough week. I did learn from it, especially in terms of how operating systems thinking actually works when you have to make something function instead of just talk about it. But I wouldn’t take Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems again. It helped me, sure, but not in the way I wanted or expected when I signed up.

text: I took CS-6250 Computer Networks as an advanced elective while working full time, so most weeks I was watching Dr. Park’s recordings late at night and piecing things together from notes and the forum rather than being “in” the class in any normal sense. I think that shaped how I experienced it more than anything else. What I still remember most is being oddly thrown in the first couple of weeks because I misunderstood one of the early report expectations and kept rereading the rubric without feeling any clearer. A forum clarification eventually fixed it, but by then I had already decided this was going to be one of those courses where I needed to triple-check every submission detail. That feeling never fully went away. The platform also had little quirks that probably shouldn’t matter, except when you are squeezing work in around a job, they absolutely do. That said, the actual assessment design mostly worked for me. It was report-heavy and definitely time-consuming, but the assignments felt like they were asking the right kinds of questions for a networks course instead of just trying to trap people on memorization. I appreciated that more than I expected, especially compared with another course I took the same term that had shorter assignments but felt much more arbitrary. Here, even when I was tired and a little irritated, I could usually see why we were being asked to analyze something a certain way after going back through the lectures. The grading comments were also pretty detailed when they arrived. “When they arrived” is the key part. text: CS-6200 was probably the class I argued with the most in my first semester, even though I weirdly looked forward to it every week. I took Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems mostly because it fit around a bunch of other hard courses, not because OS was the thing I was most excited about, and I kept up with almost every lecture. That part was actually good: the instructor explained things in a way that made kernel ideas feel surprisingly approachable, and I usually left class thinking, okay, I get why this matters. Where it got rough for me was how much weight each assignment carried. There weren’t many chances to recover, so if one project went sideways it felt huge. Late in the semester, during one of the implementation-heavy weeks, I remember finally getting a project to work at like 1:30 a.m. and feeling genuinely thrilled because the material had clicked for me for the first time. Then the grade came back lower than I expected, and I still wasn’t fully sure what the collaboration line was supposed to be versus what counted as too much discussion. A lot of us were basically relying on each other to figure out expectations, which was not ideal. I liked the instructor, honestly. The lectures were clearer than a lot of grad classes I’ve taken. But the course felt built for people who already had some adjacent systems background, and when you’re balancing multiple demanding classes, the “few assessments but each one really matters” setup can make the whole experience more stressful than it needed to be. I’m not really sure if I’d recommend it or not, but it definitely stuck with me.

text: My biggest frustration with CS-6200 was the grading. I liked the instructor fine — lectures were clear, and he was obviously trying to make OS ideas approachable — but the rubric on the projects never felt concrete enough for me to know where I was losing points, and feedback came back so late that by the time I understood what I’d done wrong, we were already deep into the next thing. That hurt more than it normally would have because the course is project-heavy and the exams matter a lot, so if you get off track early it kind of lingers. I came in with pretty strong coding experience and not much theory, which honestly is probably why some weeks felt weirdly split for me. The implementation-heavy parts were mostly doable if I stayed on top of them, but the kernel concepts took me longer than I expected to really click. I was also taking a couple other demanding classes at the same time, though the week-to-week time pressure here was usually manageable until exam periods. One thing I didn’t love was that there wasn’t much useful interaction with other students. Maybe that was partly the format, maybe just bad luck with who I ended up around, but it felt like everyone disappeared into their own work and surfaced only when they were stressed. I remember one project week where I spent more time trying to figure out whether I was overengineering a synchronization piece than actually getting help from anyone. That said, I don’t think the course itself is badly designed. For an introductory service course, it does build pretty naturally on the stated prerequisites. I struggled for most of the term and barely passed, but it never felt like I was missing some hidden background class. It was more that the evaluation side of the course made it hard to recover once I stumbled. I’d still recommend it pretty broadly, especially if you want a real introduction to operating systems and you’re okay with learning some lessons the hard way.

text: Overall I’m glad I took CS-7641 / Machine Learning, but I’d only tell someone to do it if they go in pretty prepared and have room for it. I took it mostly because people kept saying it was useful for industry work, and that part does feel true. Dr. Park’s lectures were clear, and for a summer term the pace honestly wasn’t as brutal week to week as I expected. I was taking a couple other hard classes at the same time, and most weeks the time pressure was manageable, or at least manageable enough. What I keep remembering though is how high the stakes felt because there just weren’t that many things to be graded. So each assignment/writeup mattered a lot, which made me second guess everything. The actual prereqs lined up pretty well and I never felt technically lost in the “you should have known this already” way, but I was weirdly unsure about expectations a lot of the time. especially on the writeups. Like, I could do the experiments, but then I’d spend forever wondering how much explanation they wanted, how much interpretation counted as enough, whether I was supposed to compare models in a very formal way or just justify my choices clearly. I’m still not totally sure I understood what separated an okay report from a strong one. The forums did help sometimes, and I did use them, but there were a few replies that had that slightly dismissive “it’s in the instructions” tone when the instructions were kind of exactly what felt fuzzy to me. not always, just enough that I got more cautious about asking. One small thing that stuck with me was rewriting part of a report the night before because I convinced myself my discussion section was too descriptive and not “ML enough,” which may have been me overthinking, but that was sort of the vibe of the course for me. So yeah, I learned a lot and I don’t regret it, but the workload hit harder than it looked on paper because every deliverable carried so much weight and the grading/expectation side felt less transparent than the lectures did.

text: I took CS-7641 Machine Learning with Prof. Haddad last semester before graduation mostly because it fit my schedule better than anything else. I’m not really coming from a super ML-focused background, and that mattered more than I expected. If you already know some adjacent stuff like stats/optimization or you have friends to compare notes with, the course probably lands better. I ended up only going back to the materials when I needed them, which was enough to get by, but not enough to make the flow of the class feel clear. The main thing I remember is just how assignment-heavy it felt. Not impossible, but the deadlines stacked up in a way that kept catching me off guard, especially with the writeups. A lot of my stress wasn’t even from coding, it was from trying to figure out what counted as a “good enough” analysis in the report and how detailed the expectations really were. In an ML class that gets old fast, because you can always do one more experiment or one more plot and still not know if that’s what they wanted. I had one week where I was revising graphs at like 1am mostly because the grading rubric still felt vague to me. It’s relevant in the sense that machine learning is obviously useful, but the way the course ran made it harder to appreciate. Feedback on assignments came back late enough that it didn’t help much for the next one, which was frustrating when the assignments were so frequent. That was probably my biggest complaint. I wouldn’t really recommend it unless you already have the background and a study group, because a lot of the course seemed to work better for people who could calibrate expectations together. text: I took CS-7641 Machine Learning because I needed it for my specialization, and it basically did what I expected an introductory service course to do. I mostly kept up through the recordings and the notes instead of going in person, which was fine most weeks since Prof. Rios’s slides are clear enough to follow later, even if I can barely remember any individual lecture from them now. What I remember most is being weirdly unsure about what counted as a “good enough” writeup on some of the assignments. The coding parts were usually straightforward enough, but then the report expectations felt fuzzy to me, and the feedback wasn’t super consistent from one assignment to the next. One of my writeups got pretty useful comments, and then another came back with a grade that felt harsher than I expected without really telling me what to do differently. I emailed once near a deadline when I was also drowning in another hard class, and the response eventually came, but not in time to actually help much. That was kind of the pattern when things got busy. I did like the group component more than I thought I would. Our team worked well, so the project was honestly one of the better parts of the class. I can also see how that could go the other way if your group is flaky. Prereq-wise, I think it was about what I expected. I wasn’t always confident going in, but I never felt completely out of my depth either. It helped me a lot and I’d still recommend it pretty broadly if you need a solid ML foundation, although I probably wouldn’t choose to take it again myself.

text: My main frustration with CS-6400 was honestly the grading. I liked Prof. Cohen, but the way things were graded felt harsher and less predictable than the course itself deserved, especially on the database-design assignments. A couple of times I came away thinking I understood the schema work pretty well and then lost points for choices that didn’t seem clearly signposted ahead of time. Since this was my last semester before graduation and I was fitting school around short evening study sessions, that kind of week-to-week uncertainty was the part that stuck with me most. That said, I kept up with nearly every lecture because when Prof. Cohen was on, he was really on. He explains concepts more clearly than a lot of instructors in this area, and this course built well on the prerequisites for me. Compared with the easier prereq, this one definitely asked for more actual design thinking instead of just getting through exercises, which I appreciated. I usually left lecture feeling like I understood the “why” behind normalization or a modeling choice, even if the teaching rhythm felt a little uneven from one week to the next. What helped me more than the official materials, though, was talking things through with classmates. I don’t mean that the materials were unusable, just that peer discussion was where the assignments started to click for me. One small thing I did really appreciate was that the LMS and submission process were painless, which mattered more than usual because I was often turning things in late at night after work. So yeah, mixed feelings. I was genuinely into the content and I do think Prof. Cohen knows how to make hard material understandable, but I never fully relaxed because of how the grading landed. I still remember one project where I spent way too long reworking a schema because I couldn’t tell whether I was improving it or just guessing what the rubric wanted.

text: I took CS-6400 / Database Systems Concepts and Design while working full-time, and honestly that combo kind of wrecked me by the middle of the semester. I signed up because I actually wanted to learn this stuff, not just fill an elective, and the content is useful in a very real way. I still think about some of the design tradeoffs from the writeups. but wow, I did not exactly have fun. The part that got under my skin was how much interpretation the instructions seemed to require. The project checkpoints and design writeups weren’t impossible, but I always felt like I was guessing what counted as “enough” unless I kept rereading the rubric and comparing notes with other people. This is definitely a class where having a study group helps a lot. I started the semester super engaged and went to class regularly, then once work got busy and I was also taking another hard class, my attendance kind of fell off a cliff and that made everything more annoying to piece together later. Also the software/tool setup was rough at first. not unusable, just one of those “why is this taking me 2 hours to do the first simple thing” situations. After that hump it was manageable. Exams were... fine, I guess? High stakes, not a surprise, and I wouldn’t call them unfair, but they added a lot of pressure on top of already heavy project work. So yeah, useful course, advanced enough to feel worth taking, but I was frustrated most of the time and mostly survived by leaning on classmates and stubbornness.

text: I took CS-6250 / Computer Networks with Prof. Cohen last semester before graduation, and I’m still kind of split on it. I’ve got a pretty strong coding background, so parts of the class felt doable in a practical sense, but whenever it drifted into theory-heavy explanations I was definitely less confident. I didn’t attend in a super disciplined way either — mostly I used the posted materials when I actually needed them, especially around assignments or exam prep. What I remember most is that the recorded lectures were helpful in the sense that they existed and covered what you needed, but they were also pretty dry, so I’d end up skipping around a lot. Then the assignment instructions would leave just enough room for interpretation that I’d go to the forum and find three clarification posts that basically mattered more than the original handout. That got old fast. Same with the tooling/setup stuff: I know networking courses need some environment work, but here it felt like too much effort for not that much learning payoff, at least for me. The workload was also kind of relentless. Not impossible, just frequent enough that it was always sitting in the back of my mind. Most weeks the time pressure was manageable, but it definitely had that constant deadline feeling. Weirdly, I did think the course was useful. I learned things I probably should know before graduating, and some of the networking intuition clicked better than I expected. But enjoyable? not really. My bigger issue was grading. I never felt fully clear on what would count against you versus what was just a minor implementation/detail difference, and that made the whole thing more frustrating than it needed to be. Maybe I’m being a little harsh because I took it near the end of my degree and had less patience for ambiguous rubrics by then, but I can’t honestly recommend it, even though I did get some value out of it.

text: My biggest issue with CS-6400 was honestly the grading rubrics. They always felt a little too vague for how specific the database design writeups were supposed to be, so I spent a lot of time second-guessing what counted as “enough” justification. Coming from the easier prereq, I thought this one would be a straightforward next step, but it felt less clear and more fiddly right away. That said, I took Database Systems Concepts and Design mostly because I was actually curious about how databases are structured under the hood, and I was totally new to the area, so I did get a lot out of the basics. Dr. Chen explains things in a pretty steady way, and the pacing worked better for me than I expected since I was mostly fitting school around short evening study sessions. I never felt like I had to block off an entire weekend just to keep up, which mattered a lot. The week I remember most was when the project checkpoint and another design writeup landed close together. I was annoyed because the feedback on one earlier assignment had been super useful and concrete, and then on the next one it was kind of thin, so it was hard to tell what to carry forward. The TAs were actually the thing that saved that week for me—they were responsive and practical, and when I asked a very basic question I didn’t feel talked down to. I’m still mixed on the course. The tool setup took more effort than it really paid back for me, especially as someone still learning the fundamentals, and some of the grading felt murky enough that I never fully relaxed into it. But I also can’t say it was badly taught, because parts of it were genuinely interesting and more manageable than I expected once I got into a rhythm. I probably still wouldn’t recommend it, even though I’m not sorry I took it.

text: I took CS-6400 / Database Systems Concepts and Design mostly because I was actually curious about databases and wanted a real intro. I was new to the area, so I expected basics. That was kind of the problem. The class felt like it assumed you already had more background than it said. I remember getting confused really early on, around the first SQL-heavy part, and never fully feeling caught up after that. That set the tone for the whole term for me. I had enough time overall, even while working full-time, but my motivation was on and off because every time I thought I was getting it, the course would jump ahead in a way that felt bigger than advertised. I didn’t use every resource every week, mostly dipped into the materials when I was stuck, and honestly the materials alone were not enough for me. Office hours were the main thing that kept me from totally falling behind. Those helped a lot more than the regular flow of the course. One thing I’d say in its favor: if you have a study group, this course works better. Talking through project coordination stuff with other people made a big difference. Peer interaction was probably the most functional part of the experience for me. Not even in a super social way, just practical. Compare that to another course I took the same term, where I could mostly learn solo from the lectures. Here that did not really work. Grading turnaround was pretty quick, which I appreciated, but the comments were usually too thin to tell me what to fix beyond the obvious. So I’d get a score fast and still not feel much clearer. I wanted to like this class more than I did. The topic is interesting. The course itself felt harder to enter than it needed to be.

text: I took CS-6200 / Graduate Introduction to Operating Systems in the summer, and the compressed pacing was honestly the part I remember most. I was new to this area, taking it while juggling a couple other pretty demanding classes, and I definitely had one of those semesters where I kept slipping behind on the lectures and then doing a huge catch-up sprint right before deadlines. The deadlines stacked up faster than I expected, so there were a few nights where I was still debugging a systems assignment way too late and wondering why I did this to myself. That said, I actually liked the course a lot. The instructor was clear and organized, and I never got the sense that the material was being made confusing on purpose. The recorded lectures helped a ton when I needed to catch back up, even if they could feel a little dry when I was watching three in a row. At first I thought the class was going to be more accessible to someone learning the basics, but midway through I kind of changed my mind — it’s doable, but it really works better if you already have some nearby background, because otherwise some topics hit all at once. One very specific pain point for me was spending forever chasing one bug in an assignment that turned out to be from a tiny synchronization mistake I kept overlooking. I learned a lot from that, but in the moment it was brutal. The grading itself felt fair, and scores came back surprisingly fast, which I appreciated during summer, but the feedback was sometimes just enough to know I lost points without really explaining the “why.” I also used the forums a decent amount; they were useful overall, though once or twice the replies had that “you should already know this” vibe. Still, I came out of it genuinely more interested in OS than I was going in. It was exhausting, but in a way that felt earned.
note: Instructor described as clear and organized; material not made confusing on purpose.
overall_note: Lecturer quality and increased interest are clearly positive, but the difficulty sentiment is mislabeled given the strong struggle/exhaustion described.
